t.3.1.1: Having entered the great forest, the Daṇḍaka forest, the self-possessed and invincible Rāma beheld a circle of hermitages of ascetics.
t.3.1.2: It was strewn with kuśa grass and garments of bark, enveloped in a holy, brahmic splendor, and, like the blazing disc of the sun in the sky, impossible to assail.
t.3.1.3: It was a refuge for all beings, its courtyard always well swept, and it was ever honoured and danced about by troupes of Apsarases.
t.3.1.4: Adorned with spacious fire-sanctuaries, sacrificial ladles and vessels, deerskins, kuśa grass, kindling sticks, pots of water, and fruits and roots.
t.3.1.5: The hermitage was encircled by great, sacred forest trees bearing sweet fruits; it was holy, honored with bali offerings and fire oblations, and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.
t.3.1.6: It was encircled by wild flowers and by a lotus pond full of lotuses, and by self-restrained ascetics who lived on fruits and roots and wore garments of bark and black antelope skin.
t.3.1.8: That hermitage, resembling the abode of Brahmā and resounding with the chanting of the Vedas, was adorned by illustrious brāhmaṇas who knew Brahman.
t.3.1.7: It was surrounded by ancient sages as radiant as the sun and fire, and adorned with holy, supreme seers who kept a strict restraint on their food.
t.3.1.9: Having seen that circle of ascetics' hermitages, the glorious Rāghava of great splendor unstrung his mighty bow and approached.
t.3.1.10: Those great seers, endowed with divine knowledge, seeing Rāma, then approached him with delight, and also the illustrious Vaidehī.
t.3.1.11: Seeing him like the rising moon, those sages who walked in dharma and were firm in their vows received him, pronouncing auspicious blessings.
t.3.1.12: Their faces filled with wonder, they beheld the handsome form and build, the splendor, the delicacy and the graceful attire of Rāma, the dweller in the forest.
t.3.1.13: All those forest-dwellers gazed upon Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa and Rāma, who seemed to them a marvel, as if with unblinking eyes.
t.3.1.14: There those illustrious sages, devoted to the welfare of all beings, settled him, Rāghava, as their guest in a hut of leaves.
t.3.1.15: Then those highly fortunate ones, resembling fire and devoted to dharma, having honored Rāma according to the prescribed rite, brought him water.
t.3.1.17: The king, the protector of dharma, the refuge of these people, and of great renown, is worthy of worship and honour; he is the bearer of the rod of punishment and their guru.
t.3.1.16: Having offered the great-souled one roots, flowers and forest fruits, and their hermitage as well, those knowers of dharma then spoke to him with joined palms.
t.3.1.18: O Rāghava, the king protects his subjects as though he were a fourth part of Indra; therefore, honoured by the world, he enjoys the choicest pleasures.
t.3.1.19: We, the dwellers of your realm, are to be protected by you; whether you dwell in the city or in the forest, you are our king, the lord of the people.
t.3.1.20: O king, we ascetics, rich in penance, have laid down the rod of punishment; we have conquered anger and subdued our senses. Like children in the womb, we must always be protected by you.
t.3.1.21: Having spoken thus, they honored Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, with fruits, roots and wild flowers, and with various other kinds of food.
t.3.1.22: Likewise, other ascetics, perfected ones resembling the sacred fire and of righteous conduct, duly gratified Rāma, their lord, as was fitting.
